**Duino Elegies**
Rilke's masterpiece, a cycle of ten long, philosophical elegies published in 1923. They deal with angels, death, love, and the limits of human existence. The near-universal giveaway is the opening line of the First Elegy: "Who, if I cried out, would hear me among the Angelic Orders?"

**"Beauty is nothing but the beginning of terror" and "Every angel is terrifying"**
Famous lines from the First Elegy, which says that beauty is "nothing but the beginning of terror, which we still are just able to endure," and that "Every angel is terrifying." The Second Elegy opens by repeating the idea ("Every angel is terror") and later calls the angels "Early successes, Creation's favorite ones."

**Gaspara Stampa and the First Elegy**
The First Elegy asks "Have you remembered Gaspara Stampa sufficiently yet?", referring to the Renaissance Venetian poet of unrequited love, and mentions an inscription on a tablet in the church of Santa Maria Formosa. It also describes the "night, when the wind full of space" feeds on our faces, recalls how "you walked under an open window" as "a violin yielded itself to your hearing," notes how strange it is "to no longer inhabit the earth," and ends with the mourning for Linos.

**Duino Castle, Princess Marie von Thurn und Taxis, and Château de Muzot**
Rilke began the Elegies in 1912 at Duino Castle on the Adriatic near Trieste, as the guest of his patron Princess Marie von Thurn und Taxis, to whom they are dedicated. He finished them in February 1922 in a burst of creativity (a "creative storm") at the Château de Muzot in Switzerland.

**The Tenth, Eighth, and Sixth Elegies**
In the Tenth Elegy, a young man is led through the land of Laments by an elder Lament, past the "fountain of joy," and climbs "the mountains of primal pain." It ends by saying that we, who think of happiness as rising, would feel the emotion "that almost dismays us / when a happy thing falls." The Eighth Elegy contrasts animals, which look with all their eyes into "the Open" (the unobstructed world), with humans, whose vision is turned around like "traps" set around freedom. The Sixth Elegy opens by praising the fig tree, which almost wholly omits to flower and goes straight into fruit.

**"Archaic Torso of Apollo"**
Rilke's sonnet about a headless ancient Greek statue of Apollo in the Louvre, the opening poem of the second part of New Poems (1908). It ends with the famous sudden command "You must change your life."

**"We cannot know his legendary head / with eyes like ripening fruit"**
The opening of "Archaic Torso of Apollo." The speaker says the torso is still "suffused with brilliance from inside, like a lamp," so that a smile runs through the hips "to that dark center where procreation flared." The stone glistens "like a wild beast's fur" beneath "the translucent cascade of the shoulders" and would "burst like a star," since "there is no place / that does not see you."

**"The Panther"**
Rilke's famous poem about a caged panther in Paris's Jardin des Plantes. Its gaze is so weary from the passing bars that "It seems to him there are a thousand bars; / and behind the bars, no world." Its padding gait is "like a ritual dance around a center / in which a mighty will stands paralyzed." Sometimes "the curtain of the pupils / lifts, quietly," and an image enters, "plunges into the heart and is gone."

**New Poems, "thing-poems," and Auguste Rodin**
Rilke's New Poems (1907–08) contain his Dinggedichte ("thing-poems"), which describe objects and animals with intense attention. They were inspired by his time working as secretary to the sculptor Auguste Rodin, who urged him to look closely at things. Another example is "The Spanish Dancer," in which a flamenco dancer flares up like a struck match until she is "completely fire," her naked arms whirling like "startled rattlesnakes."

**Sonnets to Orpheus**
A cycle of 55 sonnets that Rilke wrote in a few weeks in February 1922 at Muzot, as a memorial for Wera Ouckama Knoop, a young dancer who died of illness. The first sonnet opens "There rose a tree. Oh pure transcendence! / Oh Orpheus sings!" and calls the lyre-playing god a source of "new beginning, sign, and transformation."

**Lines from the Sonnets to Orpheus**
One sonnet says not to erect a monument, but to "let the rose blossom each year" for Orpheus's sake. Another praises the poet whose "mortal heart presses out / a deathless, inexhaustible wine." One addresses a dog, and the final sonnet urges "Let this darkness be a bell tower."

**Letters to a Young Poet**
Ten letters Rilke wrote between 1903 and 1908 to the young military cadet and aspiring poet Franz Xaver Kappus, published after Rilke's death. He advises Kappus to "go into yourself" and explore "the depths where your life wells forth" to decide whether he truly must write.

**The Book of Hours**
Rilke's early three-part cycle of prayer-like poems addressed to God, inspired by his journeys to Russia. Its parts are "The Book of Monastic Life," "The Book of Pilgrimage," and "The Book of Poverty and Death," and the poems are sometimes published in English as "Love Poems to God."

**The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge**
Rilke's only novel (1910), a fragmentary series of 71 journal-like entries by a young Danish nobleman living in poverty in Paris, who reflects on his childhood, fear, and death.

**Rilke's early life and other poems**
Rilke was born in Prague in 1875, and his mother called him Sophia and dressed him as a girl to make up for the loss of an earlier daughter. His early collections include Life and Songs and Offering to the Lares, which draws on Prague legends such as those of Rabbi Loew. His poem "Autumn Day" ends by saying that whoever is alone now will "wander the avenues, back and forth, restlessly, while the leaves are blowing."
